name: New Hampshire
summary_text: Visitors to New Hampshire stand under the United States national framework in every respect that touches identity documents and entry. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department no longer processes the X marker, and passports are issued only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted. Passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry, but trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application. The Supreme Court has allowed the State Department to continue this treatment, and the ACLU litigation on behalf of seven plaintiffs is pending.  Entry rules add a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25', and an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.  Within that national regime, New Hampshire carries an unusually high recorded incident load. GLAAD's 2025 national census documents 72 anti-LGBTQ incidents in New Hampshire during 2025, the second-highest count of any state after California's 198, and ahead of Texas at 66, Ohio at 50 and Washington at 50. The figure exceeds counts recorded in states with several times New Hampshire's population, which is the strongest single indicator in the sourced material of what a trans visitor may encounter on the ground.  Against that, the state's courts have applied existing civil-rights machinery to a trans victim. On 17 July 2026 the Merrimack County Superior Court found that a Concord man violated the New Hampshire Civil Rights Act by striking a transgender woman. The case establishes that assault against a trans person in New Hampshire can be pursued as a civil-rights violation and adjudicated in state court, rather than going unremedied.  Checkpoint and screening exposure follows national procedure: the National Center for Transgender Equality describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can disclose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation. Multiple foreign governments, including at least eight European countries such as Finland and Denmark, have issued or adjusted travel advisories for trans and nonbinary citizens travelling to the United States.

name: New Jersey
summary_text: A trans visitor to New Jersey is bound first by United States federal rules, which apply identically in every state. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, and new passport applications are decided only as M or F from the supporting documents submitted. Passports already issued with an X marker stay valid until expiry, but travellers whose papers no longer match their presentation can expect questions at issuance and at the border. The ACLU's lawsuit on behalf of seven plaintiffs and Lambda Legal's documentation guidance are the outstanding points of challenge, and the Supreme Court has allowed the State Department to continue its changed treatment of trans passports.  Entry carries a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, followed by the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025, requires refusal of visas to trans athletes seeking to enter to compete in women's sporting events, with applicants flagged internally under the code SWS25. The same announcement treats a declaration of a gender other than sex assigned at birth as potential fraud, carrying a permanent bar. A visitor travelling for sport should assume the rule is applied mechanically.  Checkpoint procedures risk involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as steps that can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening of the type matching one's presentation.  Inside New Jersey the measured legal environment is among the most protective in the country. The July 2026 national legal-risk assessment, built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, places New Jersey in a fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier whose laws have, in the assessment's words, gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights. On the separate state-by-state dataset of killings of trans women covering 2008 to 2025, New Jersey records 3.4 per 100,000 per year, four recorded deaths in total, and is labelled 'Safest States'.

sources.title: New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (amended 1991, 2006)
sources.documents: Prohibits discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations based on affectional or sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, including perceived orientation
sources.detail: Cited as amended in 1991 to include 'affectional or sexual orientation' and in 2006 to include 'gender identity and expression'; discussed alongside Boy Scouts of America v. Dale
